6-01:
Answer

Properties of random numbers (Banks):

  1. Uniformity: the numbers must be uniformly distributed on the interval (0, 1) — every value is equally likely, so no sub-interval is favoured.
  2. Independence: each number must be statistically independent of every other number — there must be no detectable pattern or correlation between successive values.

These two properties are exactly what the statistical tests of section 6.7 onwards check.

Why computer-generated numbers are called pseudo-random:

Because they are produced by a deterministic mathematical formula (LCM, mid-square, etc.) from a starting seed. Given the same seed and the same formula, the identical sequence is reproduced every time. Such numbers therefore only appear random and pass the statistical tests for randomness — they are not truly random. The prefix pseudo (false, apparent) states precisely this: deterministic origin, random appearance.

True randomness requires a physical source (radioactive decay, thermal noise). Its practical disadvantages are that the sequence cannot be reproduced for debugging, and it cannot be generated fast enough for a large simulation.
6-03:
Answer

Pseudo-random numbers are numbers generated by a deterministic algorithm that appear to be random — uniformly distributed on (0, 1) and independent of each other — but are completely reproducible from the seed.

Qualities of an efficient random number generator:

  1. Uniformity: the numbers must be uniformly distributed over (0, 1).
  2. Independence: no correlation between successive numbers.
  3. Long period: the sequence must not repeat within the length of any run that will be made.
  4. Reproducibility: the same seed must regenerate the same sequence, so runs can be repeated and debugged.
  5. Fast generation: each number must cost very little computation, because a simulation may need millions of them.
  6. Low memory: the generator should keep only a small amount of state between calls.
  7. Passes statistical tests: it must satisfy the uniformity and independence tests (chi-square, K–S, auto-correlation, poker, run test).
  8. Portability: it must work identically on different machines and compilers, independent of word length.
  9. Multiple independent streams: the ability to produce several disjoint streams from one generator, needed for the different random components of a model.

The Lehmer (Linear Congruential) generator and the combined LCG (L'Ecuyer) are the classical designs that satisfy these requirements; the mid-square method satisfies almost none of them.
6-04:
Answer

Pseudo-random number: a number produced by a deterministic algorithm which nevertheless passes the tests for uniformity and independence, so it behaves as if it were random. It is called pseudo because the same seed always regenerates the same sequence.

How they help in simulation:

  1. Artificial sampling: a simulation has to imitate chance events — how many customers arrive, how long service takes, which machine fails. The generator supplies the random values from which samples of these distributions are drawn (inverse transform, Box-Muller, etc.).
  2. Monte Carlo computations: the same numbers provide the sampling points that estimate integrals, areas and the value of π.
  3. Reproducibility of experiments: because the sequence follows from the seed, a run can be repeated exactly. If random results had to be reproduced with physical randomness this would be impossible to do reliably.
  4. Different independent streams: separate streams can be assigned to different random components (arrivals, service, failures), which improves the statistical quality of the study.
  5. Speed and cost: they are generated on the computer itself in microseconds, unlike tables of random digits which must be stored and are quickly exhausted.

6-06:
Answer

Several characteristic faults can arise when pseudo-random numbers are generated:

  1. Short period / cycling: the sequence repeats much sooner than required. If the period is shorter than the number of values the simulation needs, the same history is replayed and the results are biased. Example: LCM with X₀=27, a=17, c=43, m=100 has period only 4.
  2. Degeneracy (falling to a constant): the mid-square method reaches 0000 and stays at 0 for ever. The multiplicative LCM with a=13, m=26 collapses to 0 from any seed, because a and m are not coprime.
  3. Non-uniform distribution: the generated values cluster instead of filling (0, 1) evenly, so the empirical distribution differs from the uniform distribution the model assumes.
  4. Correlation between successive values (lattice structure): LCM output lies on a small number of hyperplanes in k dimensions; a poor choice of a, c and m makes this visible as structure in scatter plots.
  5. Poor low-order bits: in a straightforward LCM the least significant digits are much less random than the high-order digits, so the generator must not be used by taking only those digits.
  6. Bad seed selection: seeds such as 0 (for a multiplicative generator) or values outside the period produce a trivial or degraded sequence.
  7. Non-random dependence on the modulus: choosing m as a power of two makes the period and the pattern of the low-order bits weak; m should be a large prime or a large power of a prime with a ≡ 1 mod 4.
  8. Implementation errors: integer overflow and precision loss when the arithmetic is done in floating point produce incorrect, repeated or biased values.

These faults are why no generator may be used in a study without first passing the battery of statistical tests described in sections 6.7–6.13.
6-07:
Answer

The role of random numbers in simulation is to imitate the chance elements of a real system. Almost every stochastic simulation needs them to sample from the input distributions of the model:

  • Sampling how many customers arrive in an interval (Poisson arrivals)
  • Sampling the time between two arrivals (exponential inter-arrival times)
  • Sampling service times, machine failure and repair times, demand levels, lead times
  • Sampling the discrete events of random processes and, in Monte Carlo work, generating the sample points of a numerical estimate

The numbers are used because every such quantity is defined in terms of a uniform random number on (0, 1), transformed by the inverse-transform, Box-Muller or rejection method into the required distribution. Thus the quality of the whole simulation depends on the quality of the random number stream: if the stream is not uniform and independent, every sampled value is biased and so is the result of the study.

Answer

Algorithm for LCM:

  1. Choose the seed X₀, the multiplier a, the increment c and the modulus m (with X₀, a, c < m).
  2. Compute the next value by Xₙ₊₁ = (a × Xₙ + c) mod m.
  3. The normalized random number is Rₙ₊₁ = Xₙ₊₁/m, which always lies in [0, 1).
  4. Set Xₙ = Xₙ₊₁ and repeat from step 2 for as many numbers as needed.
  5. If c ≠ 0 the generator is called mixed congruential; if c = 0 it is multiplicative congruential (Xₙ₊₁ = a Xₙ mod m).

Multiplicative congruential with a = 13, m = 26:

Xₙ₊₁ = (13 Xₙ) mod 26

For X₀ = 2:

  1. X₁ = (13 × 2) mod 26 = 26 mod 26 = 0
  2. X₂ = (13 × 0) mod 26 = 0, and every later value is 0.

Sequence: 2 → 0 → 0 → 0 … period = 1 (degenerate).

For X₀ = 4:

  1. X₁ = (13 × 4) mod 26 = 52 mod 26 = 0
  2. All later values are 0 — period = 1 (degenerate).

Conclusion: a = 13 and m = 26 share the common factor 13, so every multiple of 13 vanishes modulo 26 and both seeds collapse to zero. The generator is worthless, which shows the general rule: in a multiplicative congruential generator the multiplier and the modulus must be chosen so that the numbers produced cycle through a long period, and a seed sharing a factor with m destroys the period. In practice m is taken as a large prime (or a large power of two with a ≡ 1 mod 4) and m must be larger than the longest run.

Answer

A combined linear congruential generator runs several congruential generators with different moduli and combines their outputs into a single stream.

For j = 1, 2, …, k, define the components:

Xj,n+1 = (aj Xj,n + cj) mod mj

Then combine them (L'Ecuyer):

Xn = ( Σj=1..k (−1)j−1 Xj,n ) mod (m1 − 1) + 1     Rn = Xn / m1

(with Rn = (m1 − 1)/m1 used if Xn = 0).

Why it is used

  1. Far longer period. The period of the combined generator is approximately the product (or least common multiple) of the component periods, so periods of the order of 1018 are reached even though each component alone has a period of only 109.
  2. Better statistical quality. Combining breaks the regular lattice structure that makes the output of a single LCM fall on a small number of hyperplanes, so the combined stream passes uniformity and independence tests that the components fail.
  3. Independent streams. The components can be advanced separately, giving several disjoint streams that can be assigned to different random components of a simulation (arrivals, service, failures) or to different processors.

Example of parameters (L'Ecuyer, 1988): m₁ = 2147483563, a₁ = 40014; m₂ = 2147483399, a₂ = 40692. Both components are multiplicative (c = 0) and the combined generator has a period of about 2.3 × 1018 — the classic generator used by many simulation packages.

Answer

The mid-square method is the earliest random number generator; it was proposed by John von Neumann in 1946.

Algorithm

  1. Take an n-digit number as the seed X₀.
  2. Square it (pad with leading zeros if necessary to obtain exactly 2n digits).
  3. Take the middle n digits of the square as the next number X₁.
  4. Use X₁ as the new seed and repeat from step 2.
  5. A random number in (0, 1) is obtained as Rₙ = Xₙ / 10n.

Example (4-digit seed 7182)

StepSeedSquareMiddle 4 digits
17182515811245811
25811337677217677
37677589363299363

Random numbers: 0.5811, 0.7677, 0.9363.

Problems

  • The sequence can degenerate to zero: once the middle digits are 0000, every later value is 0.
  • The period is short and dependent on the seed: some seeds cycle almost immediately.
  • It is not guaranteed to be uniform, and it is slower than arithmetic generators.

Because of these defects the mid-square method is of historical interest only; the linear congruential generator replaced it.

The mid-square method (von Neumann, 1946) generates a new random number by squaring the previous one and extracting the middle digits.

Method: start with an n-digit seed, square it to get a 2n-digit number, take the middle n digits as the next value, and use that as the new seed. Normalize by dividing by 10n to obtain a number in (0, 1).

Example — seed 7182 (4 digits):

StepSeedSquaredMiddle 4 digitsR = X/10⁴
171825158112458110.5811
258113376772176770.7677
376775893632993630.9363
493638766576966570.6657

Fourth number: 6657 (0.6657).

Remarks: the method needs no multiplication constants and no modulus, which made it attractive on early computers, but the period is short and depends entirely on the seed, the output is not reliably uniform, and the sequence can degenerate to zero (0000). It is therefore not used in serious simulation work.

Answer

Mid-square random number generator (proposed by von Neumann, 1946):

  1. Start with an n-digit seed.
  2. Square the seed to obtain a 2n-digit number.
  3. Extract the middle n digits — this is the next random number.
  4. Repeat, using the extracted value as the new seed. Divide by 10n to normalize.

Example with a 4-digit seed:

StepSeedSquaredMiddle 4 digits
17182515811245811
25811337677217677
37677589363299363

Problem with the generator: the sequence can degenerate. If the middle digits ever become 0000 the square is 00000000 and every subsequent value stays 0, so the generator stops producing random numbers. Other weaknesses are the very short period for many seeds, sensitivity to the choice of seed, and no guarantee of uniformity. Because of this it has been replaced by the linear congruential method.

Answer

Part 1 — Qualities of a good random number generator

  1. Uniformity: values are uniformly distributed over (0, 1).
  2. Independence: no correlation between successive values.
  3. Long period: the sequence does not repeat within the length of any run.
  4. Reproducibility: the same seed regenerates the same sequence, which is essential for debugging and for controlled experiments.
  5. Fast and cheap generation: millions of values may be required.
  6. Small memory requirement and portability across machines.
  7. Ability to provide several independent streams for the different random components of the model.

Part 2 — Methods used for testing

TestWhat it verifies
Frequency testThat values are spread evenly over (0, 1)
Chi-square testUniformity, by comparing observed and expected frequencies in k intervals
Kolmogorov–Smirnov testUniformity of the whole cumulative distribution, with no grouping
Auto-correlation testIndependence of values separated by a lag l
Run test (runs up and down)Independence, from the pattern of rises and falls in the sequence
Gap testIndependence, from the length of gaps between values in a chosen range
Poker testIndependence of the digit patterns inside each number

A generator is accepted only if it passes the whole battery, since each test is sensitive to a different kind of defect.
6-22:
Answer

An efficient random number generator must satisfy the following qualities. They fall into two groups — statistical quality and practical usability.

Statistical qualities

  1. Uniformity: the numbers must be uniformly distributed on (0, 1); no part of the interval may be favoured.
  2. Independence: each number must be independent of all the others — no correlation between successive values and none between values a fixed lag apart.
  3. Long period: the sequence must not begin to repeat until far beyond the number of values the simulation will consume, otherwise the same history is replayed and the results are biased.
  4. Passes the standard tests: frequency, chi-square, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, auto-correlation, gap, poker and run tests.

Practical qualities

  1. Reproducibility: the same seed must always reproduce the same stream, so that runs can be repeated exactly and a suspicious result investigated.
  2. Speed: generation must be fast, because a study may need millions of values; multiplication and addition only, no division or floating-point logarithms.
  3. Low memory: only a few words of state should be kept between successive calls.
  4. Portability: identical output on different hardware and compilers — the generator must not depend on the machine word length or on the outcome of integer overflow.
  5. Multiple independent streams: the ability to produce several disjoint sub-streams, one for each random component of the model.

The linear congruential generator and the combined LCG (L'Ecuyer) meet these requirements, which is why they are the generators built into standard simulation software.
6-23:
Answer

Testing of random numbers means applying statistical tests to the stream produced by a generator in order to establish that the numbers really are uniformly distributed and independent — that is, that they behave like genuine random numbers.

Why it is needed:

  1. Generator output is deterministic, so any defect in the algorithm or in the choice of its parameters produces a stream with a pattern. Such a pattern is invisible to the eye but ruins the simulation.
  2. Every simulation formula assumes uniform and independent input, e.g. xᵢ = a + (b − a)Rᵢ for sampling. If the assumption fails, every sampled value is biased and so is the final answer.
  3. The parameters a, c and m may produce a period far shorter than the length of the run (example: period 4 for X₀=27, a=17, c=43, m=100), so the same history is repeated.
  4. Some methods degenerate — the mid-square method can fall to zero, and the multiplicative generator with a = 13, m = 26 collapses immediately.
  5. It is a matter of professional responsibility: the validity of every conclusion drawn from the study rests on the quality of the random numbers, so they must be tested before the model is believed.

The tests used are the frequency, chi-square, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, auto-correlation, gap, poker and run tests.

Answer

Random numbers are tested for the two required properties — uniformity and independence — by the following methods.

TestProperty testedStatistic and decision rule
Frequency testUniformityCounts of values in k equal intervals; expected N/k. A gross check, usually replaced by chi-square.
Chi-square testUniformityχ² = Σ(Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ compared with χ²(α, k−1). If χ² < table value, accept the numbers as random.
Kolmogorov–Smirnov testUniformity (whole distribution)D = max |F_n(x) − F(x)| compared with D_α/√N. Needs no grouping, so it is stronger than chi-square.
Auto-correlation testIndependence between values a lag l apartρ̂ = (1/M) Σ Rᵢ Rᵢ₊ₗ − 0.25, then Z₀ = ρ̂ / σ_ρ̂ compared with Z_{α/2} = 1.96.
Run test (runs up and down)Independence from the order of the valuesCount the runs a, then Z₀ = (a − μ_a)/σ_a with μ_a = (2N−1)/3, σ²_a = (16N−29)/90, compared with 1.96.
Gap testIndependence, from the lengths of gapsChi-square on the observed gap lengths against the theoretical geometric distribution.
Poker testIndependence of digit patternsClassify numbers by their digit patterns (all different, one pair, three of a kind) and apply chi-square.

The tests are complementary: chi-square and K–S examine the distribution of values and ignore their order, while the auto-correlation, run and gap tests examine the order and ignore the distribution. A generator must pass both groups.
6-25:
Answer

Random numbers must be tested because the generator is a deterministic formula, so any weakness in it produces a stream with a hidden pattern, and every such weakness corrupts the simulation:

  1. All sampling in a stochastic simulation is derived from uniform random numbers (x = a + (b − a)R, inverse transform, Box-Muller). If R is not uniform or not independent, every sampled variable is biased, so arrival patterns, service times and hence the whole output of the study are wrong.
  2. A generator may have a much shorter period than the run length, so the simulation replays the same events and produces an artificially stable, over-optimistic result.
  3. A generator may produce values that are correlated (the lattice structure of a poor LCM), which makes the observations in the run statistically dependent; the confidence intervals and replication analysis of Chapter 7 then become invalid.
  4. Some methods degenerate to a constant (mid-square → 0), which silently stops the simulation from being stochastic at all.
  5. The principle is garbage in, garbage out: no amount of careful model building or statistical analysis can recover from a bad random number stream, so testing is done before the model is trusted.

The tests used are uniformity tests (frequency, chi-square, Kolmogorov–Smirnov) and independence tests (auto-correlation, run, gap, poker).
6-27:
Answer

The chi-square test is a goodness-of-fit test. In simulation it is used for two purposes:

  1. To test whether the numbers produced by a generator are uniformly distributed on (0, 1) — the uniformity half of the randomness requirement.
  2. To test whether an input distribution fitted to data (exponential, Poisson, etc.) is a good fit, which is part of validating the model's data assumptions.

Formula:

χ² = Σ (Oᵢ − Eᵢ)² / Eᵢ

where Oᵢ is the observed frequency in interval i, Eᵢ = N/k the expected frequency, N the sample size and k the number of intervals.

Steps: divide (0, 1) into k equal intervals → count the observed frequency in each → compute Eᵢ = N/k → compute χ² → compare with the table value χ²(α, k − 1). If the calculated χ² is less than the table value, the observed distribution does not differ significantly from the uniform, and the numbers are accepted as random.

Significance: it converts a visual impression ("the values look evenly spread") into a quantified decision at a stated confidence level, and it does so for the whole distribution at once. Its limitation is that the result depends on the number of intervals chosen, and it needs a reasonably large sample (Eᵢ ≥ 5 in every interval) — which is why the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test is often used alongside it.
6-28:
Answer

Chi-square test — a goodness-of-fit test used to decide whether the observed frequencies of a set of values differ significantly from the frequencies expected under a stated distribution. In random number testing the stated distribution is the uniform distribution on (0, 1).

Formula

χ² = Σ (Oᵢ − Eᵢ)² / Eᵢ     with degrees of freedom = k − 1

where Oᵢ = observed frequency in interval i, Eᵢ = N/k = expected frequency, N = number of random numbers, k = number of equal intervals.

Steps

  1. State H₀: the numbers are uniformly distributed. H₁: they are not.
  2. Divide the range into k equal intervals (a common choice is [00–19], [20–39], [40–59], [60–79], [80–99], so k = 5).
  3. Count the observed frequency Oᵢ in each interval and compute Eᵢ = N/k.
  4. Compute χ² = Σ (Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ.
  5. Obtain the critical value χ²(α, k − 1) from the table for the chosen α.
  6. If the calculated χ² is less than the table value, fail to reject H₀ — the numbers are accepted as uniformly distributed. If it is greater, reject H₀ — the numbers are not random.

Example

For 50 numbers in 5 intervals with observed frequencies 11, 9, 13, 7, 10 (Eᵢ = 10):

χ² = 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.9 + 0.9 + 0 = 2.00, and χ²(0.05, 4) = 9.488. Since 2.00 < 9.488, the numbers pass the test.

Answer

The auto-correlation test checks whether numbers separated by a fixed lag are correlated. When the question asks about the 2nd, 7th, 12th … numbers, the lag is l = 5 and only those numbers form the comparison series.

Steps

  1. Pick the numbers at positions 2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27 from the 30-value sequence.
  2. Form the M pairs of consecutive values from this series: (2, 7), (7, 12), (12, 17), (17, 22), (22, 27). Here M = 5.
  3. Compute the estimated auto-correlation
ρ̂ = (1/M) Σi=1..M (Rᵢ × Rᵢ₊ₗ) − 0.25
  1. Compute the standard deviation of ρ̂ and the test statistic:
σ_ρ̂ = √(13M + 7) / (12(M + 1))     Z₀ = ρ̂ / σ_ρ̂

With M = 5: σ_ρ̂ = √(13×5 + 7)/(12×6) = √72/72 = 8.485/72 = 0.1178.

  1. Compare |Z₀| with Z_{α/2} = Z_{0.025} = 1.96 for a two-tailed test at α = 0.05.

Decision

  • If |Z₀| ≤ 1.96, the values are not auto-correlated and the numbers are accepted as independent.
  • If |Z₀| > 1.96, the numbers are auto-correlated and the generator fails the test of independence.

The calculation of ρ̂ itself uses only the five products obtained in step 2 — multiply each pair, sum the products, divide by M and subtract 0.25. In this test the statistic is extremely sensitive to the ordering of the values, which is exactly what the chi-square test cannot see.

The auto-correlation test detects dependence between numbers a fixed distance apart. Taking the 3rd, 8th, 13th … values means the lag is l = 5, and only those values are used, so the sequence of 30 numbers yields the series R₃, R₈, R₁₃, R₁₈, R₂₃, R₂₈.

  1. Write down the five selected values in order.
  2. Multiply each value by the next one in the series (the value one lag later) and add the five products: S = Σ Rᵢ Rᵢ₊₇.
  3. ρ̂ = S/M − 0.25.
  4. Z₀ = ρ̂/0.1178.
  5. Compare with ±1.96.

Interpretation of the possible outcomes

Computed Z₀Conclusion
|Z₀| ≤ 1.96Fail to reject H₀ — the numbers are independent, no auto-correlation at lag 7.
Z₀ > 1.96Reject H₀ — the values a lag apart tend to rise and fall together (positive auto-correlation).
Z₀ < −1.96Reject H₀ — the values alternate (negative auto-correlation).

Numerical meaning of ρ̂: ρ̂ measures the correlation between the value at position i and the value at position i + 7. It is compared against the theoretical value 0.25 (the expected product of two independent uniform values) rather than against 0, which is why 0.25 is subtracted in the formula. A value of ρ̂ close to zero after this correction means no correlation; a large positive ρ̂ means the generator carries a hidden trend across the sequence, which would invalidate the independence assumption of every replication in the study.

Answer

This is the poker test, which tests independence by classifying three-digit numbers according to the pattern of their digits.

Theoretical probabilities for three-digit numbers:

  • All three digits different: P = 10 × 9 × 8/10³ = 720/1000 = 0.720
  • Exactly one pair of like digits: P = 1 − 0.720 − 0.010 = 0.270
  • All three digits alike: P = 10/10³ = 0.010

Expected frequencies for 1000 numbers: 720, 270 and 10.

CategoryObserved OᵢExpected Eᵢ(Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ
All different680720(680 − 720)²/720 = 1600/720 = 2.222
Exactly one pair289270(289 − 270)²/270 = 361/270 = 1.337
Three alike3110(31 − 10)²/10 = 441/10 = 44.100

χ² = 2.222 + 1.337 + 44.100 = 47.659

Degrees of freedom = k − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2, so at α = 0.05 the critical value is χ²(0.05, 2) = 5.991.

Conclusion: since 47.659 > 5.991, the null hypothesis of independence is rejected. The numbers are not independent. The rejection is caused almost entirely by the last category — 31 numbers with three like digits were observed where only 10 were expected — a strong sign that the generator repeats digits far too often. The generator must be replaced (or its parameters corrected) before it is used in a simulation.
6-33:
Answer

Poker test — a test of independence for random numbers which, instead of looking at the magnitude of the numbers, classifies them by the pattern of their digits and compares the observed pattern frequencies with the theoretical probabilities using the chi-square test. It takes its name from the hands of a poker game.

Method

  1. Group the random digits into numbers of d digits (commonly 3 or 5).
  2. Define the pattern classes for those numbers. For 3-digit numbers there are three classes: all digits different, exactly one pair of like digits, and all three digits alike.
  3. Compute the theoretical probability of each class. For 3-digit numbers:
    • All different: 10 × 9 × 8/10³ = 0.720
    • Exactly one pair: 0.270
    • Three alike: 10/10³ = 0.010
  4. Count the observed frequency Oᵢ of each class in the sample.
  5. Compute the expected frequencies Eᵢ = Pᵢ × N, where N is the number of numbers.
  6. Compute χ² = Σ (Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ with k − 1 degrees of freedom.
  7. Compare with the critical value and decide.

Example

For 1000 three-digit numbers with observed counts 680, 289 and 31 against expected 720, 270 and 10:

χ² = 1600/720 + 361/270 + 441/10 = 2.222 + 1.337 + 44.100 = 47.659, compared with χ²(0.05, 2) = 5.991.

Since 47.659 > 5.991 the numbers are not independent — the excess of numbers with three like digits is the cause.

Significance and limitation

The test is valuable because it detects dependence that the frequency tests cannot see: a generator can produce an evenly spread set of values whose digits are nevertheless patterned. Its limitation is that the result depends on the number of digits chosen per group, and it needs a large sample so that every expected frequency is at least 5.
